questions.stem: Under the Treaty of Portsmouth of 1905, which ended the Russo-Japanese War, Japan gained:
options: a large cash indemnity from Russia and control of all of Manchuria and Mongolia
the whole of Sakhalin, the port of Vladivostok and the Trans-Siberian Railway
Taiwan, the Pescadores Islands and the right to station troops in Beijing
the lease of the Liaodong Peninsula, southern Sakhalin and a free hand in Korea
questions.explanation: Japan gained the Liaodong lease, including Port Arthur, the southern branch of the Manchurian railway, southern Sakhalin and recognition of its dominance in Korea. Russia paid no indemnity, which angered the Japanese public. Taiwan had been gained from China in 1895.

questions.stem: Why did the Hibiya riots break out in Tokyo in September 1905?
options: Crowds were angry that the peace with Russia brought no indemnity after costly sacrifices
Workers were protesting against the conscription of factory labour for the war in Manchuria and Korea
Students were demanding a written constitution and an elected parliament for Japan
Farmers were protesting against the export of rice to feed the army in Manchuria
questions.explanation: The public had been told of great victories and had borne heavy taxes and casualties, so the lack of an indemnity at Portsmouth seemed a betrayal. The riots showed that popular opinion was becoming a force in politics. Japan already had a constitution and a Diet from 1889-1890.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains the wider significance of Japan's victory over Russia in 1905?
options: It ended all Western influence in China and left Japan as the only foreign power there
It made Japan the leading naval power in the world, ahead of Britain and the USA
It forced Russia to accept Japan as an equal partner in governing Manchuria
It was the first defeat of a European great power by an Asian state in modern war
questions.explanation: The victory astonished the world and inspired nationalists across Asia. It confirmed Japan's status as a regional power, but Western powers kept their privileges in China, and the British and American navies remained larger.

questions.stem: Japan formally annexed Korea in:
questions.explanation: Korea became a Japanese protectorate in 1905 after the Russo-Japanese War and was annexed in 1910. It remained a Japanese colony until 1945. The March First Movement for Korean independence took place in 1919.

questions.stem: In the First World War, Japan joined the Allies in August 1914 and quickly seized:
options: Germany's leased territory at Qingdao in Shandong and its Pacific islands north of the equator
Germany's colonies in New Guinea and Samoa south of the equator, then the Dutch East Indies
Russia's naval base at Vladivostok and the Russian half of Sakhalin, then the whole of northern Manchuria
Britain's naval base at Hong Kong and France's colony in Indochina, then the Philippines
questions.explanation: Japan entered the war under the Anglo-Japanese Alliance and took Qingdao in November 1914, along with the Marianas, Carolines and Marshalls. Australia and New Zealand took German New Guinea and Samoa. Japan's navy later escorted Allied convoys in the Mediterranean.

questions.stem: Japan presented the Twenty-one Demands to Yuan Shikai's government in January 1915. Their purpose was to:
options: extend Japan's control over China while the European powers were occupied by war
persuade China to join the Allied side in the war against Germany in Europe
end the unequal treaties so that China and Japan could unite against the West
secure Chinese support for Japanese claims to Germany's former colonies in the Pacific
questions.explanation: The demands sought confirmation of Japan's gains in Shandong, extended rights in Manchuria and Inner Mongolia, and, in the fifth group, Japanese advisers in the Chinese government. Japan exploited Europe's distraction, but did not seek to end Western privileges.

questions.stem: Japan dropped the fifth group of the Twenty-one Demands before issuing an ultimatum to China in May 1915. What does this best show?
options: China's army had defeated Japan, forcing it to withdraw its most important claims
Japan had decided to rely on the League of Nations to settle its future disputes with China
Japan was ambitious in China but still sensitive to pressure from Britain and the USA
Japan had abandoned its ambitions in China in favour of expansion into the Pacific
questions.explanation: The fifth group, which would have made China nearly a protectorate, caused alarm in Britain and the USA as well as China. Japan withdrew it but forced China to accept most of the rest. The episode damaged Japan's reputation and fuelled Chinese nationalism. The League did not exist until 1920.

questions.stem: At the Paris Peace Conference in 1919, Japan's proposal to include a racial equality clause in the League of Nations Covenant was:
options: blocked, a rebuff that many Japanese saw as proof of Western racism
adopted, which led Japan to become a founding member of the League
withdrawn by Japan itself after China objected to its claims on Shandong
accepted, but only for the colonial peoples governed under League mandates
questions.explanation: Although a majority of the commission voted for it, Wilson ruled that it required unanimity, with Australia's Billy Hughes among its strongest opponents. Japan still joined the League with a permanent Council seat and gained the German rights in Shandong, but the rejection fed resentment.

questions.stem: The Five-Power Treaty agreed at the Washington Naval Conference of 1921-1922 set a ratio for capital ships between the USA, Britain and Japan of:
questions.explanation: The USA and Britain could each have five tons of capital ships for every three Japanese tons, with France and Italy at 1.75. Japanese navalists resented the inferior ratio, though Japan's navy could concentrate in the Pacific while the others had wider commitments.

questions.stem: Which other outcome of the Washington Conference affected Japan's international position?
options: Japan was given a mandate over Korea, and the USA recognised Manchuria as Japanese territory
Britain and Japan renewed their alliance, and the USA agreed to leave the Philippines by 1930
China ceded Shandong to Japan, and the powers agreed to abolish all unequal treaties in China
The Anglo-Japanese Alliance was replaced by a Four-Power Treaty, and Shandong was returned to China
questions.explanation: The Four-Power Treaty ended the Anglo-Japanese Alliance, a key prop of Japan's position since 1902. The Nine-Power Treaty bound the powers to respect China's integrity and the Open Door, and Japan agreed to return Shandong. Many Japanese saw the settlement as containing Japan.

questions.stem: Hara Takashi became prime minister in 1918 and is significant because he was:
options: the founder of the Japan Communist Party and the leader of the wider labour movement
the last of the genro, who chose every prime minister until the late 1930s
the first commoner to lead a cabinet formed from the majority party in the Diet
the first army general to be appointed prime minister by the Emperor himself
questions.explanation: Hara, president of the Seiyukai, formed a party cabinet after the Rice Riots brought down the Terauchi government. He was assassinated in 1921. The last genro was Saionji Kinmochi.

questions.stem: Which reform of 1925 extended democracy in Japan?
options: The General Election Law gave the vote to all men aged 25 and over
A new constitution made the Diet, not the Emperor, the source of sovereignty
The vote was given to all adult men and women on equal terms
The House of Peers was abolished and replaced by an elected senate
questions.explanation: The 1925 law removed the tax qualification, roughly quadrupling the electorate; the first election under it was held in 1928. Women did not gain the vote until 1945-1946, and the Meiji Constitution remained in force.

questions.stem: The Peace Preservation Law was passed in 1925, the same year as universal male suffrage. Which interpretation does this pairing best support?
options: Leaders extended the vote only because the army had openly threatened to seize power if they did not
The Diet passed both laws to prepare Japan for a socialist government elected by workers
The two laws were unrelated, because the second applied only to Japan's overseas colonies
Leaders extended the vote while guarding against radicals who might use it to challenge the system
questions.explanation: The Peace Preservation Law punished anyone who organised to change the kokutai, the national polity, or abolish private property. It was used against communists, anarchists and later others, including in mass arrests in 1928. It shows the limits of Taisho democracy.

questions.stem: The zaibatsu were:
options: large family-controlled business conglomerates such as Mitsui and Mitsubishi
groups of elder statesmen who advised the Emperor on choosing prime ministers
young army officers who plotted against party politicians in the 1930s
rural tenant farmers' unions that campaigned for lower rents in the 1920s
questions.explanation: Conglomerates such as Mitsui, Mitsubishi, Sumitomo and Yasuda controlled banks, trading companies and industries. The elder statesmen were the genro.

questions.stem: How did the zaibatsu exercise political influence in the 1920s?
options: They appointed army and navy ministers, who then had to approve every cabinet decision
They elected their own members to the House of Peers as a separate business class
They controlled the genro, who could dismiss any government that raised company taxes
They funded the main parties, with Mitsui linked to the Seiyukai and Mitsubishi to the Minseito
questions.explanation: Party politics was expensive, and the parties depended on business donations. These ties led to public perceptions of corruption and money politics, which later fed hostility to both the parties and the zaibatsu.

questions.stem: In the late 1920s Japanese politics was dominated by two main parties. They were the:
options: Kodoha and the Toseiha
Kenseikai and the Genyosha
Seiyukai and the Taisei Yokusankai
Seiyukai and the Minseito
questions.explanation: The Seiyukai and the Minseito, formed in 1927 from the Kenseikai and another group, alternated in power from 1927 to 1932. The Kodoha and Toseiha were army factions, and the Imperial Rule Assistance Association (Taisei Yokusankai) replaced the parties in 1940.

questions.stem: Which statement best evaluates the impact of the Seiyukai and Minseito on the Japanese political system?
options: They had little impact, because the genro chose all ministers from outside the Diet until 1932
They made party cabinets normal, but scandal and bitter rivalry weakened public trust in them
They abolished the Emperor's powers and made Japan a parliamentary democracy on the British model
They united against the army and so prevented any military influence over cabinets until 1937
questions.explanation: From 1924 to 1932 the leader of the main party usually became prime minister, a period of 'normal constitutional government'. But the parties attacked each other bitterly, were tied to business money and were tainted by scandals, so few defended them when militarists attacked them in the 1930s.

questions.stem: Under the Meiji Constitution, how could the army challenge or bring down a party cabinet?
options: By ordering the Diet to dissolve, since the Chief of Staff controlled the election timetable
By vetoing the budget in the House of Peers, where generals held a majority of the seats
By refusing to provide an army minister, since every cabinet needed a general in that post
By calling a referendum on the cabinet's defence policy, which the Emperor had to accept
questions.explanation: The army and navy ministers had to be generals and admirals, and the services had direct access to the Emperor through the 'independence of supreme command'. Withdrawing or refusing a minister could bring down a cabinet. The active-duty requirement was relaxed in 1913 and restored in 1936.

questions.stem: The genro were:
options: senior officers of the Kwantung Army who directed policy in Manchuria and Korea
officials of the Imperial Household who controlled the Emperor's lands and income
elder statesmen outside the constitution who recommended prime ministers to the Emperor
elected members of the House of Representatives who formed the ruling party's leadership
questions.explanation: The genro were leaders of the Meiji Restoration who advised the Emperor informally. By the 1920s only Saionji Kinmochi remained, and he generally favoured party cabinets. As the genro died out, no one could balance the army, bureaucracy and parties.

questions.stem: Why did the Great Depression hit rural Japan especially hard?
options: The price of raw silk, sold mainly to the USA, collapsed along with the price of rice
Japanese farmers depended on wheat exports to Britain, which ended with imperial preference
The government seized farmland to build factories, leaving peasants without any income
A series of earthquakes destroyed the rice harvests in every year from 1929 to 1933
questions.explanation: Many farm families relied on raising silkworms for extra income, and silk exports to the USA collapsed. Rice prices also fell sharply. Rural poverty and debt spread, and many in the army, which recruited heavily from the countryside, blamed the parties and the zaibatsu.

questions.stem: In January 1930 the Minseito government returned Japan to the gold standard at the old parity. What was the consequence?
options: The zaibatsu lost all their foreign assets and were broken up by the government in 1931
Deflation and falling exports deepened the Depression, and the policy was blamed on the parties
Exports boomed because the yen was cheap, ending the Depression in Japan by the middle of 1930
Foreign banks lent Japan large sums, which it used to build up its navy beyond the treaty limits
questions.explanation: Finance Minister Inoue Junnosuke's return to gold just as world trade collapsed caused severe deflation. Japan left gold in December 1931; Takahashi Korekiyo then let the yen fall and increased spending, and Japan recovered faster than most countries.

questions.stem: Which development of the 1920s and 1930s is an example of rising social tensions caused by modernisation and urbanisation?
options: The cities emptied as factory workers returned to their villages to farm their own land
The government banned all Western films and music from Japan from the early 1920s
Rural Japan grew richer than the cities as farm prices rose throughout the 1920s
Conservatives and nationalists condemned Western-style city culture as a threat to Japanese values
questions.explanation: Cities grew rapidly, with office workers, cafes, cinemas, the 'modern girl' and the 'modern boy', and labour unions. Conservatives saw these as decadent and individualistic, while rural Japan lagged behind. This gap fed nationalist calls for a return to traditional values.

questions.stem: In the London Naval Treaty of 1930, Prime Minister Hamaguchi Osachi accepted limits on cruisers. Why did this cause a political crisis?
options: The army objected because the treaty also cut the number of divisions stationed in Manchuria
The navy general staff and nationalists claimed the civilian cabinet had infringed the supreme command
The Diet rejected the treaty, so Hamaguchi was forced to dissolve parliament and call an election
The treaty gave Japan parity with Britain, which the Emperor rejected as a threat to world peace
questions.explanation: Opponents argued that only the military's command organs, not the cabinet, could decide the forces needed for defence. Hamaguchi was shot by a nationalist in November 1930 and died the following year. The crisis weakened party control over the military.

questions.stem: On 15 May 1932 a group of young naval officers assassinated which prime minister?
options: Hamaguchi Osachi
Takahashi Korekiyo
Inukai Tsuyoshi
Hara Takashi
questions.explanation: Inukai, leader of the Seiyukai, was killed in the May 15 Incident. Hara was assassinated in 1921, Hamaguchi was shot in 1930, and Takahashi was killed in the February 26 Incident of 1936.

questions.stem: After the May 15 Incident the conspirators received light sentences, helped by a flood of public petitions for leniency. What does this best suggest?
options: The courts had been abolished and the army now tried all political cases itself
The public strongly supported party government and opposed any military role
The Emperor had ordered the release of all those who opposed the parties
Many Japanese sympathised with violent 'patriots' and had lost faith in the parties
questions.explanation: The trial became a platform for the defendants' claims of selfless patriotism against corrupt politicians and businessmen. Lenient treatment encouraged further violence. After Inukai, no party leader formed a cabinet again before the war.

questions.stem: What change followed the assassination of Inukai in 1932?
options: Party cabinets ended, and Admiral Saito Makoto led a 'national unity' cabinet
The Diet was abolished, and the Emperor ruled directly through a council of generals
The Minseito took power, and it cut military spending to pay for rural relief
The army declared martial law, and General Araki Sadao became prime minister
questions.explanation: The genro Saionji recommended Saito, a retired admiral, rather than the new Seiyukai leader, to calm the military. The Diet and parties continued to exist, but no party leader was prime minister again until after the war. Araki was army minister, not prime minister.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the two main factions in the Japanese army in the 1930s?
options: The Imperial Way faction wanted to withdraw from Manchuria; the Control faction wanted to make peace with China and the Soviet Union
The Imperial Way faction wanted an alliance with Britain; the Control faction wanted to join the League of Nations and disarm
The Imperial Way faction wanted a 'Showa Restoration' by direct action; the Control faction wanted planned mobilisation for total war
The Imperial Way faction wanted to restore party government; the Control faction wanted to replace the Emperor with a military council
questions.explanation: The Kodoha (Imperial Way), linked to Araki Sadao and Mazaki Jinzaburo, attracted young officers who wanted to purge corrupt elites, often by violence, and saw the USSR as the main enemy. The Toseiha (Control), associated with Nagata Tetsuzan and later Tojo Hideki, worked with bureaucrats and industry to prepare for total war.

questions.stem: The February 26 Incident of 1936 was:
options: the Japanese attack on Chinese troops at the Marco Polo Bridge near Beijing
the walk-out of the Japanese delegation from the League of Nations Assembly
a general strike by Tokyo workers protesting against rising military budgets
an attempted coup by young officers in Tokyo, which was put down within days
questions.explanation: About 1,400 troops led by young Imperial Way officers occupied central Tokyo and killed senior figures, including Finance Minister Takahashi Korekiyo. The revolt ended on 29 February. The Marco Polo Bridge clash took place in July 1937.

questions.stem: Which was the most significant consequence of the February 26 Incident for the army's role in politics?
options: The Imperial Way faction took over the government and abolished the Meiji Constitution
The army withdrew from politics and handed power back to the Seiyukai and Minseito
The Control faction purged its rivals and the army's influence over government grew
The army was placed under full civilian control after the Emperor dismissed its leaders
questions.explanation: The rebel leaders were tried and executed, and Imperial Way generals were retired. But the army used fear of further violence to increase its say: in May 1936 the rule that service ministers must be active-duty officers was restored, giving the army a veto over cabinets.

questions.stem: Which is an example of hostility towards the zaibatsu in the early 1930s?
options: The head of Mitsui, Dan Takuma, was assassinated by a nationalist group in 1932
The government nationalised Mitsubishi and Sumitomo after the Manchurian Incident
The Diet passed a law in 1931 dissolving the zaibatsu into small separate firms
Zaibatsu leaders were barred from voting in elections under the 1925 election law
questions.explanation: The League of Blood killed former Finance Minister Inoue Junnosuke and Dan Takuma in 1932, accusing the zaibatsu of profiting while farmers starved. The zaibatsu were broken up only under the Allied occupation after 1945, and in the 1930s they adapted by investing in Manchuria and war industries.

questions.stem: Which example best shows that responses to militarism within Japan differed?
options: All socialists and communists united behind the army after 1931 and joined the Kodoha faction
Minobe's 'organ theory' was banned in 1935, yet in 1937 voters still backed the established parties
Every newspaper opposed the occupation of Manchuria until the government closed them in 1932
The Diet unanimously voted to abolish itself in 1936 so the army could rule without opposition
questions.explanation: Minobe Tatsukichi's theory that the Emperor was an organ of the state was condemned in the Diet, and his books were banned. Yet in the April 1937 election the main parties won most seats against the army-backed Hayashi cabinet, which then resigned. Most newspapers supported the Manchurian venture.

questions.stem: Historians disagree about Emperor Hirohito's role in the 1930s. Which evidence most clearly shows that he could act decisively when he chose to?
options: He accepted the advice of the genro Saionji on who should be appointed prime minister
He insisted that the February 26 rebels be suppressed when some army leaders hesitated
He read speeches written by his ministers at the opening of each new session of the Diet
He appeared in public on a white horse at army reviews and inspected naval exercises
questions.explanation: Hirohito called the rebels mutineers and demanded they be crushed, and in 1929 his rebuke had led Prime Minister Tanaka Giichi to resign over the cover-up of Zhang Zuolin's murder. Some historians stress that he usually accepted advice as a constitutional monarch; others argue he was more involved than once believed.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the ideology promoted in documents such as the 1937 Kokutai no Hongi (Cardinal Principles of the National Entity)?
options: Loyalty to a divine Emperor and the uniqueness of Japan's national polity, against Western individualism
Individual rights, free trade and parliamentary democracy on the American and British model
Class struggle by workers and peasants to overthrow the Emperor and the zaibatsu
Peace through disarmament, membership of the League and cooperation with China
questions.explanation: Issued by the Ministry of Education, it taught that Japan was a family-state under an Emperor descended from the gods, and it condemned individualism, liberalism and communism as foreign ideas. It was used in schools to build loyalty.

questions.stem: During the 1920s, Foreign Minister Shidehara Kijuro's diplomacy aimed to:
options: drive the Western powers out of China and build a Japanese empire on the Asian mainland
form an alliance with the Soviet Union against Britain and the United States in the Pacific
withdraw Japan from all its colonies, including Korea and Taiwan, to save on defence costs
cooperate with the Western powers and expand Japan's trade with China by peaceful means
questions.explanation: Shidehara supported the Washington system, non-intervention in Chinese politics and economic expansion. Army leaders and nationalists criticised his policy as weak, and Tanaka Giichi's 'positive policy', which sent troops to Shandong, offered a firmer alternative.

questions.stem: The Manchurian Incident of September 1931 began when:
options: Soviet forces crossed the Amur River into Manchuria, and Japan sent troops to drive them back
Kwantung Army officers blew up a section of the South Manchurian Railway near Mukden and blamed China
Chinese troops attacked a Japanese garrison in Shanghai, killing its commander and seizing the whole port
the League of Nations ordered Japan to withdraw from Korea, and Japan sent troops into Manchuria
questions.explanation: Officers including Ishiwara Kanji and Itagaki Seishiro staged the explosion on 18 September 1931 and used it as a pretext to occupy Manchuria, without approval from the government in Tokyo. The puppet state of Manchukuo was declared in 1932.

questions.stem: How did Japan respond to the Lytton Report, which the League of Nations adopted in February 1933?
options: It declared war on China and Britain, which had written the report
It agreed to share control of Manchuria with the Soviet Union
It walked out of the League and announced its withdrawal from membership
It accepted the report and handed Manchuria back to Chinese administration
questions.explanation: The report found that Japan's actions were not legitimate self-defence and that Manchukuo was not a genuine independent state. When the Assembly adopted it, the Japanese delegation led by Matsuoka Yosuke walked out, and Japan gave notice of withdrawal in March 1933.

questions.stem: Which combination of factors best explains why Japan sought to expand on the Asian mainland in the 1930s?
options: A desire to spread democracy in China, pressure from the League, and the need for Christian missions
Rapid population decline, a surplus of raw materials at home, and the wish to rejoin the Washington system
Fear of Australian expansion, the end of the zaibatsu, and an alliance with Britain against the USSR
A search for resources and markets after the Depression, army ideas of total war, and Pan-Asian nationalism
questions.explanation: The Depression and Western tariffs made a self-sufficient bloc in Manchuria and China attractive. Army planners such as Ishiwara believed a future total war required secure resources, and ideas of Japan's mission to lead Asia gave expansion an ideological justification.

questions.stem: In November 1936 Japan signed the Anti-Comintern Pact with:
options: Nazi Germany
the Soviet Union
the United States
Nationalist China
questions.explanation: The pact with Germany was directed against the Communist International and, in practice, the USSR. Italy joined in 1937. It marked Japan's move away from the Western democracies.

questions.stem: Which development best shows Japan rejecting the Washington system by the mid-1930s?
options: It returned Shandong to China and signed a new treaty guaranteeing China's integrity
It joined the Four-Power Treaty and renewed its friendship with Britain and France
It accepted a new 5 : 5 : 5 ratio offered by Britain and the USA at London in 1936
It gave notice in 1934 that it would leave the naval limitation treaty, which expired in 1936
questions.explanation: Japan demanded naval parity, and when this was refused it gave notice in December 1934 and walked out of the second London conference in 1936. With the treaty limits gone, it began building new battleships. Shandong had been returned in 1922.

questions.stem: The clash at the Marco Polo Bridge near Beijing on 7 July 1937 is significant because it:
options: caused the Soviet Union to declare war on Japan
escalated into full-scale war between Japan and China
led directly to the creation of the puppet state of Manchukuo
ended with Japan's withdrawal from northern China
questions.explanation: A skirmish between Japanese and Chinese troops escalated as the Konoe government sent reinforcements and Jiang Jieshi refused to give ground. Fighting spread to Shanghai in August and to Nanjing by December. Manchukuo had been created in 1932.
